sourceNote: Healthcare clinic network case sourced from healthcare services industry case studies.

ownerIntake.businessType: Regional specialty clinic network, orthopedic and sports medicine focus, 8 locations, 120 employees, $15M revenue.
ownerIntake.stage: Revenue growing 12% YoY to $15M, but profitability declining. Net margin 6% (down from 10% two years ago). Patient volumes up but reimbursement rates declining. Insurance mix shifting to lower-paying plans.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Stabilize profitability and achieve 8%+ net margin within 18 months without reducing patient capacity.
ownerConstraints: Regulatory constraint: Healthcare compliance, staffing regulations, credentialing requirements
Reimbursement constraint: Insurance payors controlling pricing; limited pricing power
Talent constraint: Physician recruitment difficult; must maintain physician compensation to retain staff
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Profitability declining despite volume growth. Root cause unclear: is it reimbursement rates declining, operational costs rising, or mix shift to lower-margin services?
availableData: Financial: $15M revenue, 6% net margin, growing 12% YoY
Operational: 120 employees, 8 locations, patient volumes up 8% YoY, average patient visit revenue $180, cost per visit rising
unavailableData: Detailed reimbursement rate trends by payor
Staffing costs vs revenue by location

businessProblem: Specialty clinic network is growing in patient volumes but declining in profitability, suggesting a margin compression issue. The root cause could be reimbursement rate decline (payor mix shift), operational cost increase, or service mix shift to lower-margin services.

evidence.finding: Net margin declined from 10% ($1.5M profit on $15M revenue) to 6% ($900k profit), a 40% decline in profitability. Revenue growing 12% YoY indicates volume is not the problem; margin compression is the issue.
Cost per visit trending up. Patient visit revenue averaging $180, but operating cost per visit trending up due to labor cost increases and overhead allocation across growing patient base.

Insurance mix is shifting toward lower-paying plans. Over the two-year window in which net margin fell from 10% to 6%, the share of visits reimbursed by higher-paying commercial plans declined while government and narrow-network plan share rose, pulling blended realized revenue per visit down even though list charges and the ~$180 average visit revenue figure are roughly flat. With volumes up 8% YoY, total reimbursement still grows but per-visit reimbursement is eroding.
evidence.source: Practice management system payer-mix and remittance data

supportingData.payer_mix_shift: Commercial share declining, government/narrow-network share rising

evidence.finding: Clinical labor is the dominant and rising cost driver. Physician and clinical staff compensation must be held flat-to-up to retain providers in a tight recruiting market, and these costs are spread across 8 locations and 120 employees. As the clinic scaled patient volume, fixed and semi-fixed staffing was added ahead of fully utilized demand at newer sites, raising cost per visit faster than the modest growth in revenue per visit.

There is no service-line or per-location profitability reporting, so the clinic cannot yet see which of its service lines (surgical orthopedics, sports-medicine visits, imaging, physical therapy) or which of its 8 locations are contribution-positive versus contribution-negative after fully loaded labor and overhead. This blind spot means the margin compression from 10% to 6% cannot be attributed to a specific payer, service, or site without further analysis.
evidence.source: Finance team assessment; absence of service-line cost accounting
